title: Deliver a Complete Design
summary: Start with a fuzzy prompt, agree on the essentials and build a working baseline. Then spend your interview time on the decisions that matter.
body:
A system design interview is an exercise in making and communicating decisions, not naming as many technologies as possible. Your first objective is a complete system that satisfies a small, agreed scope. Improve that baseline with evidence rather than adding infrastructure by habit.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R["1. Requirements"] --> EI["2. Entities and API"]
    EI --> H["3. Working baseline"]
    H --> D["4. Deep dives"]
    D --> W["5. Close the loop"]
    D -.->|"new constraint found"| H
```

The interview moves left to right, but not strictly: a deep dive often exposes a gap in the baseline, and you return to fix it before going further. Each stage produces something the next one uses: requirements choose the entities, entities shape the API, and the API defines the requests your baseline must serve.

As a rough budget for a 45-minute interview, spend about 5 minutes on requirements, 5 on entities and API, 10–15 on the baseline, 10–15 on deep dives and the last few minutes closing the loop. Senior candidates are usually expected to reach the deep dives with time to spare and to choose them proactively.

## 1. Agree on the problem

Ask who uses the system and identify the few actions that matter most. For a notification service, creating a message and delivering it are separate requirements; marketing campaigns and template editing might be out of scope. State what you are leaving out.

Next make the important quality goals concrete. Does delivery need to happen within seconds or hours? Is losing a message worse than delivering it twice? What does the availability target cover? A requirement such as 'fast and scalable' cannot guide a decision.

## 2. Name the entities and interfaces

List the resources before designing every column: Notification, Recipient, DeliveryAttempt. Then describe the essential interface, such as `POST /notifications` with an idempotency key and `GET /notifications/{id}` for status. Derive caller identity from authentication, not an arbitrary user ID in the body.

You can refine the data model while tracing requests. Avoid spending the opening minutes listing profile fields that do not affect the design.

## 3. Draw a working baseline

Trace one write from the caller to durable storage and one read back to the caller. For asynchronous work, trace acceptance, processing, acknowledgement and status updates. Label arrows with what travels across them and identify which component owns each piece of state.

An API, a database and a worker can be a better starting point than a dozen microservices. If you claim a request succeeded, explain what has been durably recorded at that point. A diagram without an end-to-end request is not yet a working design.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["Caller"] -->|"POST /notifications"| API["Notification API"]
    API -->|"insert, status=pending"| DB[("Notifications DB")]
    API -->|"enqueue id"| Q[["Delivery queue"]]
    Q --> W["Delivery worker"]
    W --> P["Email or SMS provider"]
    W -->|"record attempt"| DB
    C -->|"GET /notifications/id"| API
```

This baseline for the notification example records the request durably before returning, hands delivery to a worker through a queue, and lets the caller poll status from the same database. It is deliberately plain. Its weak spots become the deep dives: the API writes to the database and the queue separately, so one can succeed without the other (an outbox fixes that), and the worker may call the provider twice after a timeout (an idempotency key fixes that).

## 4. Deep-dive where requirements create pressure

Choose two or three issues that follow from the agreed goals. A notification system might need provider retry policies, tenant isolation and duplicate suppression. Explain the baseline's limitation, compare alternatives, choose one and state its cost.

Use estimates when they change a decision. If a queue receives 2,000 messages per second and workers drain 1,500, the backlog grows by 500 messages per second. That calculation identifies a real problem. Calculating storage totals without using them to choose anything does not.

## 5. Close the loop

Revisit each requirement. Identify what the design guarantees, what it only attempts, and what remains unresolved. Describe an operational check: queue age, duplicate rate or failed deliveries. Invite the interviewer to challenge an assumption rather than talking past their feedback.

## A practice routine

Choose a case study and set a timebox appropriate to your interview. Work through requirements, entities, interfaces, baseline and deep dives on paper or your own whiteboard before reading the walkthrough. Say your reasoning aloud. Afterwards, write down one missed requirement, one unsupported assumption and one tradeoff you would explain differently.

Do not treat a reference design as the only correct answer. A different datastore or architecture can be valid if its guarantees satisfy the same requirements. A quiz checks a particular concept; it does not certify interview readiness.

## Try it

For a service that sends password-reset emails, write three requirements and trace one request. Where is the durable record? What happens if the provider accepts the email but its response is lost? Keep the first design small enough that you can explain the entire flow.

## Further reading

- [Google SRE book: Service Level Objectives](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/) shows how to turn vague quality goals into measurable targets.
- [Designing Data-Intensive Applications](https://dataintensive.net/) is a thorough reference for the trade-offs behind most deep dives.
keyTakeaways: Agree on scope and measurable quality goals before choosing infrastructure.
Define entities and interfaces, then trace a complete baseline design.
Use estimates and deep dives to resolve specific requirements, not as rituals.
Practise aloud before reading a walkthrough and evaluate your reasoning, not just component names.
